Hey guys, long time LOTR fan here. i was wondering how many of you have heard about J.R.R Tolkien's intrest in the legend of Atlantis? I find it very intresting that his nightmares as a child about the destruction of the fabled continent, which he himself believed to be memories of a past life. I believe from reading his quotes that the legend of Atlantis in it self was also something in which he drew the inspiration to write the beloved LOTR series.

Truth is indeed stranger then fiction.
Where Tolkien drew his inspiration from?
Tolkien was influenced by many different sources from Beowulf to Shakespeare which is apparent from many scenes in the LOTR trilogy.

I'm sure if he was alive today he couldn't name every little thing that gave him some inspiration for certain events, characters, or symbols, but for something so epic a huge part of it would have been somewhat influenced by some past experience or literature in some small way.

Actually there is a lot of correlation between Tolkein and Wagner's The Ring of the Nibelungen cycle. Tolkein refuted this his whole life, but after watching some of the old movies of the opera, my doubts arise. The Nibelungen of course comes from the old Norse and Germanic legends, and if you ever read the Prose Edda when it names the dwarves individually, it becomes very clear where Tolkein got some of his inspiration. For example (read the numbered verses). Without a doubt, Tolkein has a lot of basis in the old Norse and Germanic myths.

I also recall a documentary which has an analysis of Tolkein's work as an analogy to his time in the world war. Can't remember the name of it, but it made some pretty good points such as England representing the Shire, etc.

The legend of the lost city of Atlantis is echoed in The Akallabeth, which is the Downfall of Numenor, wherein a mighty civilization caused their own destruction due to their increasing hubris. The gods sank their island into the sea and very few few escaped to tell the tale.

You can read some of his correspondence with friends and family where he talks briefly about the parallels between Numenor and Atlantis.

But overall, according to himself and his son Christopher, he was influenced by Nordic and Germanic legendary, as @nul pointed out above.

As well, @nul makes the great point that a lot of his writings were a reaction to the horrors he witnessed in Europe's first great mechanized war.

Numenor does indeed draw from the idea of Atlantis, just as the Dwarves and Elves draw from old Germanic, Celtic, and Slavic mythos. The Dwarves in particular are very German. The Rohirrim are taking elements of the Scandinavians and Arabs.

One must remember that pure muse does not exist. Everything we have seen and done influences who and what we are, and what we do.

As a well read man who studied histories, mythos, and language Tolkien was well suited to creating a world of his own.

A large part of the backstory of the world that Lord of the Rings takes place in is covered in the Silmarillion. And in that you can see very German stories. Clearly while he was inspired by all that was around him, the core of his world was a Germanic one. The entire werewolf/great wolf arc feels right at home along side Grendel and Beowulf.

One of the less well-known influences is the Mabinogion,
